🔑 Specialist Study: 📜 Isaiah 44:21-28 📜 The Cosmic Song of Heaven, Earth, Mountains, Forests, and Every Tree, YHWH the Womb-Former Who Stretcheth the Heavens Alone, The Blotting Away of Sin beneath the Redeemer’s Hand, the Overthrow of Diviners & False Tokens, the Confirmed Counsel of Prophetic Messengers, the Deep Commanded to Dry, Rivers Withdrawn by Divine Word, and Cyrus Named as the Shepherd of Providence for the Rebuilding of Yerushalayim & the Temple - 
❕️❕️ See QUOTE SHARE FOR THE PREVIOUS VERSES TO CATCH UP IF YOU NEED TO❕️❕️

🔑📜 VERSE + COMMENTARY STARTS HERE/NOW 📜🔑

📜 Isaiah 44:21

“¶ Remember these (O Iacob and Israel) for thou art my seruant: I haue formed thee: thou art my seruant, O Israel: thou shalt not be forgotten of me.”

📝 Commentary

After the long idol critique, YHWH turns again to Ya‘aqob.

The command is:

“Remember.”

The idolater failed because he did not set reality to heart.

Yisra’el must therefore remember the difference between Creator and created thing.

Then YHWH repeats:

“I formed thee.”

The theological contrast could not be sharper.

Humans form idols.

YHWH forms Yisra’el.

The servant is not forgotten because the Maker remembers what He formed.

This is one of Scripture's great answers to exile psychology.

A scattered people may feel abandoned.

YHWH says:

“thou shalt not be forgotten of me.”

Divine memory becomes covenant security.

📜 Isaiah 44:22

“I haue blotted out, as a thicke cloude, thy transgressions, and as a cloud, thy sinnes: returne vnto me, for I haue redeemed thee.”

📝 Commentary

Isaiah 43:25 already said YHWH blots out transgression.

Now the metaphor becomes atmospheric.

Sin is like:

thick cloud,
cloud cover.

YHWH removes it.

The sky clears.

This is meteorological soteriology.

Transgression is imagined as something obscuring light.

Forgiveness becomes atmospheric clearing.

Then notice the order:

“Return unto me, for I have redeemed thee.”

Redemption provides the ground for return.

The restored relationship is rooted in Divine action.

This verse also prepares the cosmic song that immediately follows.

Once the cloud of sin is removed, heaven and earth erupt into praise.

📜 Isaiah 44:23

“Sing, O yee heauens: for the LORD hath done it: shout yee lower parts of the earth: breake foorth into singing yee mountaines, O forrest and euery tree therein: for the LORD hath redeemed Iacob, and glorified himselfe in Israel.”

📝 Commentary

This is one of Isaiah's great cosmic liturgies.

The command addresses:

heavens
lower parts of earth
mountains
forest
every tree

Creation itself is summoned into worship.

The phrase “lower parts of the earth” is particularly striking. At minimum it expresses the deepest terrestrial regions in contrast with heaven above. Within later biblical and Christian interpretive traditions, “lower parts” also becomes language capable of carrying underworld resonance, as in Ephesians 4:9.

Thus the hymn spans vertical reality:

above,
below,
mountain,
forest.

This is a genuinely multidimensional doxology.

Psalm 148 offers the great canonical parallel, where angels, heavenly hosts, sun, moon, stars, dragons, deeps, fire, hail, snow, vapour, mountains, trees, beasts, kings, and peoples are summoned into one cosmic praise.

Redemption therefore produces effects beyond the isolated human soul.

It becomes a cosmic announcement.

📜 Isaiah 44:24

“Thus saith the LORD thy redeemer, and he that formed thee from the wombe; I am the LORD that maketh all things, that stretcheth foorth the heauens alone, that spreadeth abroad the earth by my selfe:”

📝 Commentary

This is one of the strongest Creator declarations in Isaiah.

YHWH is:

Redeemer,
Womb-Former,
Maker of all things,
Heaven-Stretcher,
Earth-Spreader.

The scale moves from womb to cosmos in one breath.

The same Divine Intelligence forms individual embodied life and stretches the heavens.

This is extraordinary microcosm-macrocosm theology.

Then comes:

“alone”
“by myself.”

No rival creator assists Him.

No idol shares the work.

No celestial being supplies missing capability.

Angelic hosts exist within creation, not alongside YHWH as co-authors of creation.

And within the Christian canon, this verse becomes enormously important when read beside:

John 1:3:

“All things were made by him.”

Colossians 1:16:

“by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible.”

Hebrews 1 applies Creator-language from the Psalms to the Son.

Thus Christian Scripture places Yeshua within the very Creator-side of the Creator-creature distinction Isaiah guards so fiercely.

This is why Isaiah 44:24 belongs among the most important Old Testament texts for Creator Christology.

The One Isaiah calls YHWH who stretches the heavens alone is identified canonically with the creative agency of the Son.

That is a far deeper claim than simply calling Yeshua a prophet or heavenly messenger.

📜 Isaiah 44:25

“That frustrateth the tokens of the lyers, and maketh diuiniers mad, that turneth wisemen backward, and maketh their knowledge foolish:”

📝 Commentary

Now the Creator confronts rival systems of supernatural and intellectual authority.

The verse names:

tokens
liars
diviners
wise men
knowledge

Isaiah is not denying that ancient societies practiced divination, omen-reading, dream interpretation, astral observation, necromancy, and ritual consultation.

The ANE world was saturated with them.

Mesopotamian omen literature could interpret:

celestial events,
animal entrails,
birth anomalies,
dreams,
weather,
eclipses,
planetary configurations.

Isaiah's claim is hierarchical.

YHWH can frustrate signs, overthrow divinatory expectation, and reverse the conclusions of experts.

The Creator stands above every semiotic system operating within creation.

Daniel 2 supplies a magnificent parallel.

Babylon's wise men cannot reveal Nebuchadnezzar's dream, but Daniel receives the mystery from the God of heaven.

The issue is ultimately revelatory jurisdiction.

Who owns the hidden thing?

Daniel answers:

“there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets.”

📜 Isaiah 44:26

“That confirmeth the word of his seruant, and performeth the counsell of his messengers; that saith to Ierusalem, Thou shalt be inhabited; and to the cities of Iudah, Yee shall be built, and I will raise vp the †decayed places thereof.”

📌 1611 Marginal Remark

† Heb. wastes.

📝 Commentary

Verse 25 frustrates false signs.

Verse 26 confirms true prophetic speech.

This contrast is essential.

YHWH:

frustrates false tokens
but
confirms His servant's word.

Prophecy therefore is distinguished from divination by source and covenantal authority.

The “counsel of His messengers” evokes the world of prophetic commission, but the word messenger, Hebrew mal’akh, is also the ordinary term for angelic messenger depending on context.

Here the immediate reference is best understood of YHWH's prophetic messengers, yet Isaiah's larger world contains both human and celestial messengers functioning under Divine command.

The deeper principle is:

YHWH's counsel becomes effective through commissioned agents.

Then prophetic word becomes architecture:

Yerushalayim inhabited.

Cities rebuilt.

Wastes raised.

The speech of God literally reconstitutes ruined space.

This is logomorphic restoration, Word becoming built environment.

📜 Isaiah 44:27

“That saith to the deepe, Be drie, and I will drie vp thy riuers.”

📝 Commentary

This verse returns to primordial and Exodus-like waters.

Hebrew tehôm, “deep,” is one of Scripture's ancient cosmological terms.

Genesis 1:2 gives:

“darkness was upon the face of the deep.”

The Deep belongs to the primal waters over which the Spirit of God moved.

Now YHWH speaks directly to the deep:

“Be dry.”

Again creation responds to speech.

This recalls:

Exodus 14 and the Red Sea,
Joshua 3 and Jordan,
Psalm 106,
Nahum 1, where waters dry before YHWH,
Revelation 16, where the Euphrates is dried.

The Deep is not autonomous chaos.

It answers the Creator.

In ancient Near Eastern cosmologies, primordial waters could be imagined through divine or monstrous figures. Biblical theology repeatedly subordinates the waters to YHWH without presenting Him as struggling for uncertain victory.

He speaks.

The deep obeys.

That is hydro-cosmic sovereignty.

📜 Isaiah 44:28

*“That saith of Cyrus, He is my shepheard, and shall performe all my pleasure, euen saying to Ierusalem, Thou shalt be built, and to the Temple, Thy foundation shall be laid.”

📌 1611 Side References

The page points toward:

2 Chronicles 36:22
Ezra 1:1
Isaiah 45:13

📝 Commentary

The chapter ends with one of biblical prophecy's most remarkable historical declarations:

Cyrus.

A foreign imperial ruler is called:

“my shepherd.”

That title is striking because shepherd-language elsewhere belongs to kings, Davidic rulers, YHWH Himself, and ultimately Messiah.

Cyrus is not thereby made Messiah in the full Christological sense, but he becomes an extraordinary providential shepherd-instrument.

Isaiah 45 will go even further and call him YHWH's anointed, Hebrew māshîaḥ.

The chronology is astonishing within the literary world of Isaiah because Cyrus is named as the ruler through whom Jerusalem and the Temple will be restored.

2 Chronicles 36 and Ezra 1 later present Cyrus issuing the decree permitting Temple rebuilding.

Thus prophecy moves from:

Creator of heaven,
Ruler of deep waters,
Confounder of diviners,
Confirmer of prophets,

directly into the naming of an earthly king.

This is the chapter's final demonstration that YHWH's sovereignty operates through every scale:

womb
Spirit
human identity
heavenly hosts
time
matter
craftsmanship
clouds
heavens
earth
divination
prophecy
deep waters
imperial rulers
cities
Temple foundations

Cyrus thinks and acts historically.

Isaiah reveals a providential layer beneath history.

A Persian king becomes an instrument in the restoration of Zion.

🔑 Deep Architecture of Isaiah 44

Isaiah 44 is one of Scripture's great chapters of ontological sorting.

It asks the reader to distinguish:

the Creator from the crafted,
the Spirit from dryness,
the Rock from unstable images,
the heavenly King from earthly rulers,
true prophecy from divination,
Divine counsel from human prediction,
living covenant identity from self-manufactured religion.

Its supernatural architecture is enormous.

YHWH of Hosts presides above celestial companies and every created power.

The First and the Last stands across the whole sequence of generations.

The Spirit is poured like floodwater upon the covenant seed.

The Rock has no equal.

The heavens are stretched by YHWH alone.

The earth is spread by His own power.

The lower parts of the earth join heaven, mountains, forests, and trees in the cosmic Song of Redemption.

The Deep hears a direct command and dries.

Diviners and omen-readers can have their signs frustrated by the One who governs the realities from which signs are derived.

Prophetic messengers speak words YHWH subsequently performs.

Cyrus, though an imperial king, becomes YHWH's shepherd within providential history.

And from a Christian canonical perspective, the chapter's deepest correspondence may be the convergence of Isaiah 44:6 and 44:24:

YHWH says:

“I am the first, and I am the last.”

Revelation places that title upon Yeshua.

YHWH says:

“I am the LORD that maketh all things, that stretcheth forth the heavens alone.”

John, Colossians, and Hebrews place the Son within the act of creation itself.

Thus the Emmanuel and Messiah theology of Isaiah does not terminate with a merely human royal agent.

Across the full canon, Yeshua stands within the identity-language, Creator-language, Saviour-language, Rock-language, Glory-language, and First-and-Last language reserved for YHWH.

Isaiah 44 therefore becomes one of the great canonical chambers where Pneumatology, Angelology, Divine-Council Theology, Cosmogenesis, Creator Christology, Prophetic Foreknowledge, Sacred Hydrology, Eschatological Restoration, and the Omnipotent Kingship of YHWH converge in a single chapter.

📜 Isaiah 44:1-28 📜

🔑 Specialist Study on YHWH the King & Redeemer of Yisra’el, the LORD of Hosts & the Heavenly Council, the First & the Last, the Rock beside Whom There Is No God,( no God but God the Father) the Ontological Folly of Fashioned Idols, the Blotting Out of Sin like a Cloud, the Cosmic Song of the Redeemed, The Spirit Poured upon the Seed of Ya‘aqob, the Creator Who Stretcheth the Heavens Alone, Commandeth the Deep, The Netherworld, Mtns. Trees break forth in singing, Confoundeth Diviners, Confirmeth His Messengers, & Summoneth Cyrus by Name

The 1611 chapter heading gives the broad structure:

“1 God comforteth the Church with his promises. 7 The vanitie of Idoles. 9 and folly of Idolmakers. 21 He exhorteth to praise God for his redemption and omnipotencie.”

Isaiah 44 is one of the most concentrated chapters in the entire book for pneumatology, Divine kingship, host-language, heavenly sovereignty, creation theology, prophetic foreknowledge, anti-idolatrous ontology, redemption, cosmic praise, and providential government over kings.

The chapter also forms a remarkable bridge from Isaiah 43. Isaiah 43 ended with Yisra’el under reproach. Isaiah 44 begins immediately with election, Spirit, water, blessing, and restored identity.

📜🙏📜VERSE + COMMENTARY STARTS HERE/NOW -  SEE NEXT POST REPLIES BELOW FOR FULL CHAPTER AFTER READING THE FIRST 20 VERSES HERE ON THIS POST OUT OF THE 28 TOTAL(THE REST IN NEXT POST) FOR ISAIAH 44 - THANKS - 

- STUDY STARTS - 

📜 Isaiah 44:1

“Yet now heare, O Iacob my seruant, and Israel whom I haue chosen.”

📝 Commentary

The opening words are already merciful:

“Yet now hear.”

Isaiah 43 ended with sin, sanctuary judgment, and reproach. Yet the covenant address continues.

YHWH still says:

“my servant”
“whom I have chosen.”

Judgment has not erased election.

The verb hear is especially important after Isaiah 42 and 43, where blindness and deafness became metaphors of spiritual perception. The chapter begins by reopening the auditory channel.

The servant who failed to hear is commanded again:

Hear.

This is a theology of restored receptivity.

Divine correction aims toward renewed hearing rather than annihilation of relationship.

The election language also connects Isaiah 41:8:

“Israel, art my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen.”

Across these chapters, YHWH continually returns Yisra’el to the identity that precedes its instability.

Human behavior fluctuates.

Divine covenant purpose supplies continuity.

📜 Isaiah 44:2

“Thus saith the LORD that made thee, and formed thee from the wombe, which will helpe thee: Feare not, O Iacob my seruant, and thou Iesurun, whom I haue chosen.”

📝 Commentary

The language enters the womb.

YHWH is:

the One who made
the One who formed from the womb
the One who helps

This is a theology of prenatal Divine formation.

The Hebrew root יָצַר - yātsar, “form,” is the potter-word used for shaping clay. Here the human community itself is pictured as having been shaped by YHWH before emergence into historical maturity.

Jeremiah 1:5 provides the personal prophetic parallel:

“Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee.”

Psalm 139 likewise describes the hidden development of the body beneath Divine perception.

Then comes the rare name:

Jeshurun, Hebrew Yeshurûn.

It is an affectionate covenant designation for Yisra’el, used also in Deuteronomy 32 and 33. It likely carries the sense of upright one or beloved covenant people.

Thus Ya‘aqob, whose history contains crookedness, is addressed by a name associated with uprightness.

That is covenant teleology.

YHWH addresses His people according to what His formative purpose intends them to become.

And again:

“Fear not.”

Fear is answered with three foundations:

creation, formation, election.

📜 Isaiah 44:3

*“For I will powre water vpon him that is thirstie, and floods vpon the drie ground: I will powre my spirit vpon thy seede, and my blessing vpon thine offspring:”

📌 1611 Side References

The photographed page points toward:

Isaiah 35:7
Joel 2:28
John 7:38
Acts 2:18

📝 Commentary

This is one of Isaiah's greatest pneumatological verses.

The parallelism is deliberate:

water upon the thirsty
floods upon dry ground

corresponds to:

Spirit upon thy seed
blessing upon thine offspring

Physical hydrology becomes a visible analogy for spiritual outpouring.

The Hebrew verb שָׁפַךְ - shāphakh, “pour out,” is important because the Spirit is depicted through abundance, descent, diffusion, saturation.

This is not a tiny drop of Divine assistance.

It is inundation.

Joel 2:28 later gives:

“I will powre out my Spirit vpon all flesh.”

Acts 2 explicitly cites Joel during Pentecost.

John 7:37-39 brings water and Spirit together when Yeshua cries:

“If any man thirst, let him come vnto me, and drinke.”

John then interprets the living-water imagery as referring to the Spirit.

Thus Isaiah 44 belongs to the great canonical river of:

water → Spirit → life → offspring → renewal.

The dry ground is important phenomenologically.

Dryness has no self-generated capacity to become a floodplain.

The transformation must arrive from beyond its present condition.

This is why the image works so powerfully for spiritual restoration.

The barren state does not dictate the future state.

The Rûaḥ of YHWH can create a new condition.

📜 Isaiah 44:4

“And they shall spring vp as among the grasse, as willowes by the water courses.”

📝 Commentary

The Spirit's effect becomes botanical.

The seed of Yisra’el springs up.

Again Isaiah uses vegetation to describe spiritual and communal renewal.

Willows by watercourses possess continual access to moisture. Their growth is therefore not episodic survival but sustained flourishing.

This recalls Psalm 1:

the righteous is like a tree planted by rivers of water.

Ezekiel 47 later describes trees beside the sanctuary river whose leaves do not fade.

Revelation 22 brings the motif to its final form with the river of life and tree of life.

Isaiah 44 therefore gives us a miniature theology of pneumatic botany:

Spirit descends as water.

Human community becomes vegetation.

Divine blessing appears as growth.

What was dry becomes rooted beside living flow.

📜 Isaiah 44:5

“One shall say, I am the LORDS: and another shall call himselfe by the name of Iacob: and another shall subscribe with his hand vnto the LORD, and surname himselfe by the name of Israel.”

📝 Commentary

This verse is deeply concerned with identity, naming, inscription, and voluntary belonging.

One says:

“I am YHWH's.”

Another takes the name Ya‘aqob.

Another writes or subscribes with his hand unto YHWH.

Another adopts the name Yisra’el.

The phrase “subscribe with his hand” is particularly fascinating.

It suggests written self-dedication, almost covenantal inscription.

A person's hand becomes the instrument by which allegiance is outwardly marked.

Compare Revelation's theology of names and marks:

the servants of God bear His Name upon their foreheads.

Isaiah 43 had already said:

“I have called thee by thy name, thou art mine.”

Isaiah 44 reverses the direction beautifully:

YHWH says “Thou art mine.”

The restored person responds:

“I am YHWH's.”

Divine claim awakens human confession.

This is covenant reciprocity through onomastics.

📜 Isaiah 44:6

*“Thus saith the LORD the king of Israel and his redeemer the LORD of hostes, I am the first, and I am the last, and besides me there is no God.”

📌 1611 Side References

The page connects this with:

Isaiah 41:4
Isaiah 48:12
Revelation 1:8
Revelation 1:17
Revelation 22:13

📝 Commentary

This verse is one of the chapter's theological summits.

Several Divine titles accumulate:

YHWH
King of Yisra’el
Redeemer
YHWH of Hosts
First
Last

Each title opens a different dimension of Divine sovereignty.

YHWH the King

The covenant people ultimately belong beneath Divine kingship.

Human monarchy is secondary.

YHWH the Redeemer

The King is also Go’el, Kinsman-Redeemer.

The transcendent Sovereign takes up the intimate legal role of family defender and restorer.

YHWH of Hosts

Hebrew:

יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת - YHWH Tseva’oth

“Hosts” can include heavenly armies, celestial attendants, and organized forces under Divine command.

This title belongs naturally beside:

1 Kings 22, where Micaiah sees YHWH upon His throne with the host of heaven standing around Him.

Psalm 89, where YHWH is feared in the assembly of holy ones.

Job 1-2, where the sons of God appear before YHWH.

Daniel 7, where innumerable heavenly ministers surround the Ancient of Days.

Revelation 5, where myriads of angels encircle the throne.

Thus “YHWH of Hosts” places the King of Yisra’el above an ordered celestial government.

The heavenly council is real.

Its members are subordinate.

The Host does not dilute monotheism. It displays the abundance of created celestial agency beneath the one Sovereign.

Then:

“I am the first, and I am the last.”

Revelation places this Isaianic title upon Yeshua.

Revelation 1:17:

“I am the first and the last.”

Revelation 22:13:

“I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last.”

Within Christian canonical theology, this is one of the strongest bridges between Isaiah's Divine identity-language and the identity of Yeshua.

Isaiah assigns the title to YHWH.

Revelation speaks it through Christ.

That correspondence belongs at the very center of high Christology.

📜 Isaiah 44:7

“And who, as I, shall call, and shall declare it, and set it in order for me, since I appointed the ancient people? and the things that are comming, and shall come? let them shew vnto them.”

📝 Commentary

YHWH again challenges every rival claimant through prophetic sovereignty.

The significant phrase is:

“set it in order.”

History is treated almost as something capable of arrangement, ordering, sequence, narration.

YHWH claims authority over:

past appointment,
present declaration,
future emergence.

The “ancient people” place covenant history deep within time.

No rival power can present an equivalent chronology of sovereign action.

This resembles Isaiah 41's courtroom challenge:

show the former things, declare what is coming.

The issue is not simply prediction as spectacle.

It is temporal authorship.

Anyone may guess.

YHWH declares because history itself lies within His ordering purpose.

📜 Isaiah 44:8

*“Feare yee not, neither be afraid: haue not I told thee from that time, and haue declared it? yee are euen my witnesses. Is there a God besides me? yea, there is no †God, I know not any.”

📌 1611 Marginal Remark

† Heb. rocke.

📝 Commentary

The 1611 margin is extremely important.

The main text says:

“there is no God.”

The Hebrew alternative gives:

“there is no Rock.”

Hebrew צוּר - tsûr, rock, becomes a Divine title expressing stability, protection, endurance, covenant reliability.

Deuteronomy 32 repeatedly calls YHWH the Rock.

1 Samuel 2:2 asks:

“neither is there any rock like our God.”

Psalm 18 calls YHWH the Rock and fortress.

Paul later says in 1 Corinthians 10:4:

“that Rocke was Christ.”

That correspondence is enormous within Christian canonical reading.

Isaiah asks:

Is there any Rock besides YHWH?

Paul identifies the wilderness Rock with Christ.

Again the New Testament does not place Yeshua alongside YHWH as a second rival deity.

It places Him within the Divine identity and saving presence.

The closing phrase:

“I know not any”

is almost astonishingly ironic.

If the omniscient God says He knows of no rival god, the claim is absolute.

The heavenly host exists.

Angelic powers exist.

Principalities and dominions exist.

Yet none occupies YHWH's ontological category.

This is the critical distinction between Divine council plurality and Divine uniqueness.

Many heavenly beings.

One uncreated YHWH.

📜 Isaiah 44:9

“¶ They that make a grauen image are all of them vanitie, and their †delectable things shall not profit, and they are their owne witnesses, they see not, nor know: that they may be ashamed.”

📌 1611 Marginal Remark

The margin gives the sense of their desirable or valued things.

📝 Commentary

The idol-makers now become their own witnesses.

That phrase is important after verses 7-8, where YHWH's people are His witnesses.

There are therefore two witness communities:

YHWH's witnesses testify to Divine acts.

Idol-makers testify unintentionally to the weakness of what they themselves manufacture.

The image cannot see.

The image cannot know.

The people who make it gradually participate in that same perceptual failure.

Psalm 115 explicitly says those who make idols become like them.

This is mimetic worship ontology:

worship shapes the worshipper toward the qualities of the object adored.

A living God produces awakened perception.

A blind image leads toward blindness.

📜 Isaiah 44:10

“Who hath formed a God, or moulten a grauen image that is profitable for nothing?”

📝 Commentary

The key verb is formed.

YHWH formed Yisra’el from the womb.

The craftsman forms a supposed god.

That is the inversion.

True formation flows:

Creator → creature.

Idolatry reverses it:

creature → “creator.”

The human being makes the object, then asks the object for salvation.

Isaiah exposes the contradiction by using the same language of formation on opposite sides of the ontological divide.

📜 Isaiah 44:11

*“Behold, all his fellowes shall be ashamed: and the workemen, they are of men: let them all be gathered together, let them stand vp; yet they shall feare, and they shall be ashamed together.”

📝 Commentary

The phrase:

“they are of men”

is devastatingly simple.

The craftsmen belong to the human order.

Their products cannot spontaneously ascend beyond the ontology of their makers into true deity.

The image originates within:

human intention,
human muscle,
human tools,
human material supply.

Yet the people later bow before what emerged from their workshop.

Isaiah has effectively reconstructed the entire causal chain and shown where the alleged deity entered it:

at no point.

📜 Isaiah 44:12

*“The smith ||with the tonges both worketh in the coales, and fashioneth it with hammers, and worketh it with the strength of his armes: yea he is hungry, and his strength faileth: he drinketh no water, and is faint.”

📌 1611 Side Notes

The page connects this material with Jeremiah 10:3 and Wisdom 13:11.

📝 Commentary

This verse is one of Isaiah's finest pieces of anthropological irony.

The man making the god grows:

hungry,
thirsty,
weak,
faint.

The supposed deity depends upon a mortal craftsman who cannot even complete his work indefinitely without food and water.

Isaiah 40 declared that YHWH:

“fainteth not, neither is weary.”

Isaiah 44 gives the reverse image:

the artisan creating the idol faints.

Thus the maker's exhaustion becomes evidence against the supposed divinity of the thing made.

Wisdom 13 develops similar critique in its reflection on artisans who carve wood and then pray to their own workmanship.

There is also a profound energy hierarchy here.

The craftsman expends metabolic energy.

The idol receives shape passively.

YHWH gives strength to the faint.

These are completely different causal orders.

📜 Isaiah 44:13

“The carpenter stretcheth out his rule: he maketh it out with the line: he fitteth it with planes, and he marketh it out with the compasse, and maketh it after the figure of a man, according to the beautie of a man, that it may remaine in the house.”

📝 Commentary

Isaiah now gives an extraordinary catalogue of ancient technical craftsmanship:

rule,
line,
plane,
compass.

The idol is generated through geometry.

Measurements determine its boundaries.

Human proportion determines its shape.

Aesthetic preference determines its beauty.

Then it is stationed in a house.

This becomes deeply significant beside Isaiah's creation theology.

YHWH in Isaiah 40 measured waters, spanned heaven, weighed mountains.

The carpenter also measures, but only because he inhabits a creation already structured by measure.

Human geometry is derivative.

Divine cosmometry is primordial.

The idol cannot transcend the line and compass by which it was produced.

YHWH transcends the created geometry He established.

📜 Isaiah 44:14

“He heweth him downe cedars, and taketh the Cypresse and the Oke, which he ||strengtheneth for himselfe among the trees of the forrest: he planteth an Ashe, and the raine doth nourish it.”

📌 1611 Marginal Remark

|| Or, taketh courage.

📝 Commentary

Now Isaiah follows the idol backward into ecology.

Before idol there was tree.

Before tree there was rain.

Before rain there was YHWH's created order.

The supposed god therefore depends upon a chain it did not create.

Rain nourishes the tree.

Human hands cut the tree.

Craftsmanship alters the tree.

Only afterward does the human declare part of it divine.

The satire is theological, but it is also causal analysis.

Isaiah asks the reader to follow matter backward toward its true source.

Once one traces causes far enough, the idol disappears and the Creator remains.

📜 Isaiah 44:15

“Then shall it bee for a man to burne: for he will take thereof and warme himselfe, yea he kindleth it and baketh bread: yea he maketh a God, and worshippeth it: he maketh it a grauen image, and falleth downe thereto.”

📝 Commentary

The same material serves three functions:

fuel,
oven heat,
deity.

That is the absurdity Isaiah wants the reader to feel.

One piece warms the body.

Another bakes bread.

Another receives worship.

No ontological transformation occurs between the pieces.

Only human designation changes.

This is one of Isaiah's most incisive studies in how consciousness can project sacred status onto material objects.

The same wood remains wood.

The human mind alters its interpretation.

Thus idolatry involves misassigned ontology.

📜 Isaiah 44:16

“He burneth part thereof in the fire; with part thereof he eateth flesh: he rosteth rost, and is satisfied: yea he warmeth himselfe, and saith; Aha, I am warme, I haue seene the fire.”

📝 Commentary

Isaiah deliberately slows down and lets us watch ordinary domestic life.

Fire.

Food.

Warmth.

Visual perception.

“I have seen the fire.”

The man correctly understands the first portion of wood as fuel.

His senses work normally.

That makes the later error more striking.

He is capable of seeing fire, feeling warmth, eating food, and reasoning practically.

Yet the same cognitive faculty fails when religion enters.

Isaiah therefore presents idolatry as selective epistemic breakdown rather than lack of intelligence.

A person can reason competently in daily life while becoming metaphysically confused in worship.

📜 Isaiah 44:17

“And the residue thereof he maketh a God, euen his grauen image: he falleth downe vnto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth vnto it, and saith; Deliuer me, for thou art my God.”

📝 Commentary

The climax is the prayer:

“Deliver me.”

That is especially significant because Isaiah 43 declared YHWH the only Saviour.

The person now asks manufactured residue to perform the unique Divine function of salvation.

The causal inversion is total:

the human delivered the wood from the forest, shaped it, stabilized it, and now asks the wood to deliver him.

Isaiah's argument reaches beyond ridicule into soteriology.

The ultimate question is:

What kind of being can actually save?

The answer requires real agency.

The object receiving prayer possesses none.

📜 Isaiah 44:18

“They haue not knowen, nor vnderstood: for he hath †shut their eyes, that they cannot see; and their hearts, that they cannot vnderstand.”

📌 1611 Marginal Remark

† Heb. daubed.

📝 Commentary

The blindness theme from Isaiah 42-43 returns.

Eyes exist.

Hearts exist.

Yet perception is sealed.

The 1611 marginal “daubed” gives a vivid sensory image, as though the eye has been smeared over.

This is a condition of noetic opacity.

The heart in Hebrew anthropology includes reasoning and understanding.

Thus the verse describes a failure at both sensory and interpretive levels.

Compare Romans 1, where idolatry is accompanied by darkened understanding.

Compare 2 Corinthians 4, where blindness concerns perception of Divine glory.

Biblical epistemology repeatedly warns that spiritual error can become self-reinforcing.

What one worships shapes what one becomes capable of seeing.

📜 Isaiah 44:19

“And none †considereth in his heart, neither is there knowledge nor vnderstanding to say; I haue burnt part of it in the fire, yea also I haue baked bread vpon the coales thereof: I haue roasted flesh and eaten it; and shall I make the residue thereof an abomination? shall I fall downe to †the stocke of a tree?”

📌 1611 Marginal Remarks

† Heb. setteth to his heart.
† Heb. that which commeth of a tree.

📝 Commentary

The key phrase is:

“setteth to his heart.”

The failure is not lack of available evidence.

All the evidence sits directly before the worshipper.

He handled the wood.

He burned it.

He cooked upon it.

He ate because of it.

Yet he never performs the final act of reflection.

This is a powerful ancient theory of cognition:

experience without reflection does not guarantee wisdom.

The heart must “set” the facts together.

The question Isaiah wants the man to ask is painfully simple:

How can the residue of my fuel become my God?

The tragedy is that he never asks it.

📜 Isaiah 44:20

“He feedeth of ashes: a deceiued heart hath turned him aside, that he cannot deliuer his soule, nor say; Is there not a lie in my right hand?”

📝 Commentary

This is one of the deepest psychological verses in the chapter.

“He feedeth of ashes.”

Ashes are what remain after substance has been consumed.

To feed upon ashes is therefore a metaphor of attempting nourishment from what cannot sustain life.

Then:

“a deceived heart hath turned him aside.”

The heart has become both victim and instrument of deception.

Finally:

“Is there not a lie in my right hand?”

The idol is physically held.

The evidence of deception is literally within reach.

Yet perception fails.

This is proximal blindness.

A person can hold the false object in his own hand and remain unable to name it false.

The right hand that should signify agency and power now carries deception.

Compare Isaiah 41, where YHWH holds Yisra’el's right hand.

The two images are striking opposites:

one hand is held by YHWH.

Another hand holds a lie.

Ryūgū

From the photo frame
a picture of a friend and me, smiling —
I took it down.
A darkness of sorrow comes rushing in.
In its place,
I display the shuin*
of the Holy Kannon Bodhisattva,
said to have come
from the Ryūgū of Urashima Temple.
The temple crest of butterflies,
Kannon's form
riding upon a turtle.
Kannon-sama,
in that distant Crystal Palace,
is a moon-viewing feast being held?
Sparkling,
at the bottom of the sea,
does each character of the sutra
light the lamp of the Dharma
and pour down like rain?
I, on this shore,
can only long for
the white waves of Watatsumi.***
Slipping free from that crest,
riding upon a butterfly,
let us steal the moon —
quietly —
and offer it to Otohime-sama.**
Let us shatter this darkness,
melt it into light,
and steep this body
in the galaxy
that dwells in the great sea turtle's eye.

*A shuin is a hand-stamped and hand-written seal collected at Japanese temples and shrines, often given as proof of pilgrimage.

**Ryūgū is the undersea Dragon Palace of the Urashima Tarō legend; Otohime is the dragon king's daughter who rules there.

***Watatsumi (綿津見) names both the sea itself and the Shinto sea spirit who inhabits it — an animistic presence rather than a singular, monotheistic "God."

text:
WALKING THROUGH THE WORD

Week Five: Jesus Cleanses the Temple

John 2:13–25

Come and See: A Journey Through the Gospel of John

Understand the text. See Christ clearly. Obey what God has said.

PRIMARY TEXT

John 2:13–25, CSB

Read John 2:13–25 carefully before beginning the study. Keep the entire passage together as you read. Jesus enters the temple during Passover, confronts what He finds there, answers a challenge to His authority by speaking about the destruction and raising of the temple of His body, and then encounters people who believe because of His signs. John closes by telling us that Jesus knows what is within every person.

Those events are connected. John is continuing the work he began in the opening chapter: showing us who Jesus is so that we may believe in Him.

BIG IDEA

Jesus enters His Father’s house with the authority of the Son, points to His death and resurrection as the decisive sign of that authority, and reveals that He knows the human heart completely. John calls us beyond fascination with what Jesus can do to faith in who Jesus is.

SETTING THE CONTEXT

Week Four ended at a wedding in Cana. Jesus turned water into wine, and John told us why the miracle was important. It was the first of His signs. Through it Jesus revealed His glory, and His disciples believed in Him.

John now moves from Cana to Jerusalem and from a wedding celebration to Passover.

Passover remembered God's deliverance of Israel from slavery in Egypt. Jewish pilgrims traveled to Jerusalem to worship and offer sacrifices, which helps explain the presence of cattle, sheep, doves, and money changers around the temple. Sacrificial animals were necessary within Israel's worship, and travelers needed practical ways to obtain appropriate animals and exchange currency.

John does not accuse these merchants of charging dishonest prices, nor does he say that buying a sacrificial animal was itself sinful. We should not add accusations the passage does not make.

Jesus identifies the problem Himself. His Father’s house has been turned into a marketplace.

That description immediately raises the stakes of the scene because Jesus calls the temple His Father’s house. John has already identified Jesus as the eternal Word who became flesh and as the Son who makes the Father known. Jesus now enters the temple speaking and acting with an authority that belongs to the Son.

The question is no longer simply what is happening in the temple. The question is who has just entered it.

WALK THROUGH THE TEXT

1. THE SON ENTERS HIS FATHER’S HOUSE
John 2:13–17

Jesus enters the temple complex and sees merchants selling the animals used for sacrifice along with money changers conducting their business. He makes a whip from cords, drives out the sheep and cattle, scatters the money changers’ coins, overturns their tables, and commands the dove sellers to remove their birds.

John gives no picture of Jesus losing control. His actions are deliberate and directed.

We sometimes read this scene primarily as proof that anger can occasionally be righteous. There is truth in recognizing that Jesus can confront evil without sinning, but that is too small an interpretation of what John is showing us. The passage is centered on Jesus’ identity and authority.

Jesus explains His action through His relationship with the Father. This is His Father’s house.

The disciples then remember Psalm 69, where zeal for God's house consumes the faithful sufferer. Their memory of Scripture helps them begin interpreting what they have witnessed. Jesus’ concern is not personal inconvenience. His zeal is directed toward the honor of His Father.

There is also a shadow in the language the disciples remember. Zeal will not merely motivate Him. It will consume Him. Opposition to Jesus will grow as His ministry continues, eventually leading to the cross.

Jesus therefore stands in the temple not merely as a critic of religious practice. The Son has entered His Father’s house and acted according to His authority.

WRITE THIS DOWN: Jesus does not borrow authority from the temple. The temple belongs to His Father, and the Son has entered the house.

2. THE QUESTION BECOMES ONE OF AUTHORITY
John 2:18

The Jewish authorities respond by asking Jesus for a sign demonstrating His right to act this way.

We should read their response carefully. John has not yet developed the level of hostility we will encounter later in the Gospel. Their question arises from the extraordinary nature of what Jesus has just done. If He claims the authority to disrupt activity in the temple, what sign establishes His right to do so?

They ask for evidence of authority. Jesus answers their question, but His answer reaches far beyond what they expect. He points toward His death and resurrection.

3. JESUS IS SPEAKING ABOUT THE TEMPLE OF HIS BODY
John 2:19–21

Jesus tells them that the temple will be destroyed and that He will raise it in three days.

His hearers misunderstand Him because they think He is talking about the physical structure surrounding them. Their response about forty six years of construction shows how impossible His statement sounds when understood only in architectural terms.

John does not leave his readers wondering what Jesus means. He tells us plainly that Jesus is speaking about the temple of His body.

That explanation reaches backward into what John has already taught us. In the opening chapter, the eternal Word became flesh and dwelt among us. God has come near in the person of His Son. Now temple language is applied directly to Jesus’ body.

The temple had occupied a unique place in Israel's covenant life as the place associated with God's presence, sacrifice, priesthood, and worship. Jesus is announcing that something greater than the building is standing before them. Access to God and the saving purposes represented by the temple are reaching their fulfillment in Him.

This does not give Christians permission to speak contemptuously about Judaism or the temple. Jesus Himself is Jewish, He has come to Jerusalem for Passover, and the temple belongs to His Father. John is showing fulfillment in Christ, not giving us an excuse for contempt toward the people and history through whom God brought the Messiah into the world.

The authorities asked Jesus to establish His authority with a sign. His answer is the death and resurrection of His own body. That means Jesus has not changed the subject. The resurrection will answer the question.

WRITE THIS DOWN: When Jesus is asked to prove His authority, He points ahead to the empty tomb.

4. THE RESURRECTION HELPS THE DISCIPLES UNDERSTAND
John 2:22

The disciples hear Jesus’ words, but they do not yet understand their full meaning.

John tells us that after Jesus was raised from the dead, they remembered what He had said. Then they believed the Scripture and Jesus’ word.

This gives us an important picture of how the disciples grow. Their faith is not based on pretending they understand everything immediately. They hear Jesus before they fully comprehend Him. They remember His words. They continue following Him. Later, after His resurrection, events illuminate words that had previously puzzled them.

That is different from careless faith. Jesus does not ask His disciples to stop thinking. John repeatedly invites his readers to examine testimony, signs, Scripture, words, and events. The disciples themselves are learning how those pieces fit together.

There will be times when we encounter something in Scripture that we do not yet understand. Our responsibility is neither to fake certainty nor to dismiss what we have not yet grasped. We remain students of Christ. We keep reading, thinking, praying, and submitting what we know to what God has revealed.

WRITE THIS DOWN: Mature faith does not require pretending to know everything. It requires remaining teachable under the Word of Christ.

5. SEEING SIGNS IS NOT THE END OF FAITH
John 2:23–25

John now returns to signs.

During Passover, many people see the signs Jesus is performing and believe in His name. If we stopped reading there, we might assume John was describing the same kind of response we saw from the disciples at Cana. John does not let us stop there.

Jesus does not entrust Himself to them because He knows them. There is even a striking connection in John's wording: the language translated as their believing and Jesus not entrusting Himself comes from the same Greek verb.

John is creating tension deliberately. We should not solve that tension by carelessly declaring that every individual in the crowd was consciously pretending to believe. John does not give us enough information to examine each person that way. He does show that a response produced by signs can remain inadequate. Jesus knows something about these people that outward enthusiasm cannot reveal.

The signs are doing what signs do. They are attracting attention and pointing toward Jesus. But seeing something extraordinary is not the same as understanding who Jesus is.

This theme will continue throughout John's Gospel. Some people want bread. Others want miracles. Some are amazed. Some become curious. Some follow temporarily. John keeps pressing beneath those responses toward the kind of belief that receives Jesus for who He truly is.

The closing sentence explains why Jesus cannot be fooled by appearances. He knows what is in humanity. John has moved from Jesus knowing what is happening in His Father’s house to Jesus knowing what is happening inside the human heart.

GOVERNING MOVEMENT

The passage develops through a single movement centered on the identity of Jesus.

At Cana, Jesus revealed His glory through a sign. In Jerusalem, He enters His Father’s house and exercises the authority of the Son. When challenged to establish that authority, He points toward His body, His death, and His resurrection. His disciples will understand those words more fully after He rises. The crowds respond to His signs, but Jesus sees beneath their visible response because He knows what is within humanity.

John does not allow the temple, the signs, the disciples, or the crowds to become the final subject. Each part of the passage brings us back to Jesus. The temple tells us something about Him. The resurrection will vindicate Him. The signs point toward Him. And He knows the people standing before Him better than they know themselves.

GOD

God is not indifferent to worship. Jesus’ zeal for His Father’s house shows us the seriousness with which the Son regards the honor of the Father.

Yet the passage takes us beyond the temple courts. God has drawn near in His Son. What the temple represented finds its fulfillment in Christ, particularly through His death and resurrection.

God also knows humanity completely. There is nothing hidden from Christ. He does not evaluate people by reputation, enthusiasm, religious vocabulary, or public appearance. He sees the heart without distortion.

That knowledge would be terrifying if the Son had come only to condemn sinners. John's Gospel will show us something far greater. The One who knows humanity completely has come to save.

US

Religious activity can place us near the things of God without guaranteeing that our hearts belong to Him.

That warning needs careful application. A modern church building is not the Jerusalem temple, so this passage should not be turned into rules about what activities may occur inside a church facility. John is making a much larger claim about Jesus.

We should instead ask whether the practices of our faith are actually leading us to Christ. We can read Scripture while resisting what it says. We can attend worship while protecting areas of our lives from Christ's authority. We can become interested in Christianity because of what we hope God will provide. We can admire Jesus while resisting the surrender He requires.

John will not let outward response settle the question. Jesus knows what is within us. That removes any usefulness in pretending before Him. The secret resentment, hidden sin, mixed motive, unanswered question, genuine desire, and struggling faith are already known. Christ does not need our performance. He calls for our faith.

GOSPEL

Jesus' answer to the authorities carries us toward the heart of the Christian message. They ask for a sign validating His authority, and Jesus points toward the destruction and raising of His body. The cross and resurrection are already on the horizon.

Humanity's deepest problem is not inadequate religious activity. Sin has placed us under judgment before a holy God, and no amount of outward religion can reconcile us to Him.

John has already introduced Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. Now Jesus speaks about His body being destroyed and raised. Those truths will eventually meet at the cross.

Jesus will give Himself for sinners and rise from the grave. His resurrection will not merely demonstrate that something miraculous happened. It will vindicate the identity and authority of the One who stood in the temple and spoke of raising His body.

The crowds in Jerusalem remind us that it is possible to be amazed by Jesus without yet understanding the gospel. Saving faith does not terminate at the sign. It rests in Christ.

WRITE THIS DOWN: The signs are witnesses. Jesus is the Savior. Do not confuse what points to Him with the One in whom you must place your faith.

EXAMINE YOUR HEART

John closes this passage by telling us that Jesus knows what is within humanity. That makes personal examination unavoidable, but the questions should arise from what John has actually shown us.

Ask yourself whether your Christian habits are leading you toward Christ or whether familiarity has allowed you to operate without seriously listening to Him. Consider how you respond when His Word challenges something you would prefer to keep. Examine whether your interest in Jesus depends mainly upon what you hope He will do for you.

Then consider the disciples. They did not understand everything immediately. If you are wrestling with a genuine question, you do not need to manufacture an answer simply to appear confident. Continue following Christ while bringing that question under His Word.

Finally, consider what it means that Jesus already knows you. Confession does not provide Christ with information He lacked. It brings into the light what He already sees and allows us to approach Him without pretending.

PRACTICE THIS WEEK

Read John 2:13–25 more than once this week and follow John's argument from beginning to end. Do not stop with the overturned tables. Watch how the challenge to Jesus’ authority leads to His statement about His body, how that statement leads toward resurrection, and how John finally brings the discussion to belief and the human heart.

Examine one regular part of your Christian life, whether prayer, Scripture reading, worship, service, or church attendance. Ask a simple question: is this practice helping me know and obey Christ, or have I become satisfied merely with performing the practice?

Bring one concealed struggle honestly before God in prayer. Jesus already knows it. Confess sin where confession is needed, ask for wisdom where understanding is incomplete, and obey what Scripture has already made clear.

STUDY QUESTIONS

1. Why does John tell us that this event occurred during Passover?
2. What legitimate purposes did sacrificial animals and currency exchange serve for people traveling to Jerusalem?
3. What does Jesus reveal about Himself by calling the temple His Father’s house?
4. Why is it inadequate to reduce this passage to a lesson about righteous anger?
5. Why do the Jewish authorities ask Jesus for a sign?
6. What does John tell us Jesus means by “this temple”?
7. How does Jesus’ resurrection answer the challenge to His authority?
8. Why does John tell us that the disciples understood Jesus’ words after the resurrection?
9. What tension does John create between the people believing in Jesus and Jesus not entrusting Himself to them?
10. What does the ending teach us about Jesus’ knowledge of humanity?
11. How can religious familiarity exist without genuine surrender to Christ?
12. What has John 2:13–25 shown you about Jesus that should change the way you follow Him?

CLOSING TRUTH

John began this section with Jesus entering the temple and ends it with Jesus examining the human heart. Between those two moments, the identity of Christ becomes clearer.

He is the Son who calls the temple His Father’s house. He is the One whose body will be destroyed and raised. His resurrection will vindicate the authority being challenged in Jerusalem. His signs draw people toward Him, yet He knows whether their response reaches beneath amazement.

That leaves us with more than a lesson about temple commerce or religious reform. John places Jesus before us and asks us to deal with who He is.

The same Christ who sees through every outward appearance will eventually give His body for sinners. He knows the human heart and still continues toward the cross. Our hope therefore cannot rest in appearing religious enough to impress Him. It rests in the crucified and risen Son who already knows us and calls us to believe.

CLOSING PRAYER

Father, thank You for making Yourself known through Your Son. Give us reverence for Your holiness and keep our worship centered upon You. Guard us from becoming so comfortable with religious habits that we stop listening to Christ.

Teach us to submit to the authority of Jesus even when His Word confronts what we would rather protect. Give us patience when we do not yet understand everything and humility to remain teachable. Where there is sin, lead us to repentance. Where there are honest questions, give us wisdom. Where our faith has become shallow, draw us beyond fascination with Your works into deeper trust in Your Son.

Thank You that Jesus knows us completely. Nothing in us is hidden from Him, yet He came to save sinners. Thank You for His death and resurrection and for the forgiveness and life found in Him.

Shape our worship, our thinking, and our obedience around Christ. Help us see Him clearly in Your Word and follow Him faithfully.

In Jesus’ name, amen.

NEXT WEEK

Week Six: You Must Be Born Again
John 3:1–21

John has just told us that Jesus knows what is within humanity. The next person we meet is Nicodemus, a Pharisee and ruler of the Jews who comes to Jesus at night. His opening words reveal that he has been paying attention to Jesus’ signs.

Jesus takes the conversation beneath signs, status, education, and religious achievement. Nicodemus has come prepared to discuss what Jesus can do. Jesus will address what Nicodemus needs God to do in him.

He must be born again.

text:
In 1987, Miami did something no school had ever done. They signed a deal with Nike to outfit every single sport on campus. The first university in America to do it.

They wore that swoosh for 27 years. Those were the years that built the legend. The swagger, the camo, the national titles, the teams everybody in the country loved to hate. That was Miami in its Nike era.

Then in 2015 they left, taking a 12-year Adidas deal worth around $90 million. About $6.5 million a year in cash. At the time it was the biggest apparel contract the athletic department had ever signed, and the longest deal Adidas had ever given a college program.

And then Miami stopped being Miami.

The Hurricanes spent most of that decade irrelevant. Not "The U." Just a program with great history and nothing current to point at.

In December 2021, Mario Cristobal left the University of Oregon to come home.

That detail matters more than it sounds. Oregon isn't just a Nike school. Nike is headquartered there, the company's founder built the athletic department into what it is, and no program in America is more tied to the brand. Cristobal walked away from the single most Nike-connected job in college football to take over an Adidas school that hadn't mattered in years.

Last season, Miami played for the national championship.

They lost that game to Indiana, but the point had been made. The Hurricanes were a real program again, recruiting at the top of the sport, back in the conversation every week.

Which brings us to this week.

Miami is going back to Nike. A 10-year contract worth more than $200 million, starting with the 2027 season. Around $20 million a year, roughly $13 million of it in straight cash, the rest in apparel.

That more than triples what Adidas was paying them.

Adidas made a counteroffer. It wasn't close enough.

Outside of Nike's unique arrangement with Oregon, this is believed to be the largest annual payout Nike has ever given a college program. The extra money is expected to go toward athletic department costs, NIL support, and possibly a new on-campus football facility.

Eleven years ago Miami left Nike because Adidas offered them more.

Now Nike is paying three times as much to get them back, because of what one coach built in four years.

As one radio host put it after the news broke, it isn't a stretch to say Mario Cristobal has been worth hundreds of millions of dollars to the University of Miami.

Cristobal hates when people say the U is back. He prefers to say the U is here.

Nike just paid $200 million to agree with him.

🇺🇸 🇨🇦 🇪🇺 Trump threatens Europe with tariffs and a trade cutoff if Canada becomes an “associate” of the EU

Donald Trump warned Wednesday that he will slap heavy tariffs on Europe, and could even cut off some trade with the continent, if he judges the plan to make Canada an “associate member” of the European Union a hostile act, while Mark Carney keeps posing in Strasbourg without offering Quebec anything more than a photo.

In Charlotte, North Carolina, the U.S. president answered Ursula von der Leyen’s offer without hedging. He called the idea “laughable,” branded Canada a “terrible trade partner,” and tied his response to Brussels’ intent: if the intention is good, fine; if it is bad, “very heavy tariffs” will hit Europe, and Washington could stop trading with it in certain sectors. The Associated Press and The Canadian Press report the same remarks, made on the same day the White House also signed a memorandum to strip Canadian goods out of U.S. federal procurement.

Von der Leyen issued the invitation during her State of the Union address, with Carney in the room as a guest of honour. “Associate member” does not exist in European law. No one has yet explained whether it would mean voting rights, free movement, regulatory alignment or just another communiqué. A summit planned for late October is supposed to put words on a label. In the meantime, CETA, the Canada–EU trade deal negotiated a decade ago, is still not ratified by about ten member states.

The numbers do not pose. Goods and services trade between Canada and the United States exceeds $850 billion. With the European Union, the figure is about $150 billion. Four decades of North American integration were not invented by a speech in Strasbourg. Aluminum, lumber, autos, hydroelectricity and a large share of Quebec’s plants still live off that corridor. An “alliance for the future” does not replace a customer that buys seven times more.

Carney built his brand on standing up to Trump. Canadians followed him. The problem is what comes next. Ottawa matches tariffs dollar for dollar, multiplies the trips and the talking points, then sits and listens while Brussels invents a title that has never existed, even as Washington tightens the vice — and now threatens not only Ottawa, but the whole European market. That is not sovereignty. That is staging. Quebec does not need a federal prime minister collecting European podiums while its industrial sectors pay for a trade war Ottawa can neither settle nor contain.

Trump is playing his usual game: pressure, the market, American national interest first. You can dislike the style. You cannot pretend he is the only one defending his own. Europe wants minerals, energy and a spare partner. Canada wants a plan B. Quebec needs a plan A that starts from its geography, its plants and its right to decide for itself — not a symbolic jump seat in a union it will never join.

If Brussels’ intention is commercial and limited, Trump said that could pass. If he sees a political end-run, he has already named the price: heavy tariffs and, if need be, a cutoff of trade with Europe. Between those two poles, Carney still has not said what Quebec actually gains, besides one more photograph. https://t.co/U0g5DPeYTP
